title: The ledger of hours
hook: we guard our money closely and hand out our time to anyone who asks

segments.voice: Yesterday: Seneca, who said life isn't short, only wasted. Your line was long enough, if used. Did you find the hour you gave away? Where did it go? Day thirty-one.

Imagine a stranger walks up and asks for twenty dollars. No reason. You'd say no, probably without thinking. Now imagine a stranger asks for twenty minutes. A survey, a sales call, a meeting that could have been an email, a video that autoplays into the next one. Most of us hand those over all day long. Seneca noticed the same strange double standard two thousand years ago, in the same essay we started yesterday. We guard our money. We give our time to anyone who asks.
screen: `TWENTY DOLLARS? NO.` → `TWENTY MINUTES? SURE.` → `WE GUARD THE WRONG THING.`

segments.voice: In the third chapter of On the Shortness of Life, Seneca paints the picture. People won't let anyone take an inch of their land, he says. A boundary dispute and they're off to court with stones and weapons. But they let others walk right into their lives, and even invite them in. Nobody hands out their money, but everybody hands out their life. We're tight-fisted with property, and wildly generous with the one thing it would be right to be stingy with: time. Then he does something clever. He imagines a man who's reached old age, and asks him to go through the ledger. Take your years, he says, and subtract. How much went to a creditor, how much to a patron you had to flatter, how much to quarrels at home, how much to running errands around the city? Subtract all that, and you'll find you have fewer years than you've counted. Seneca makes the same point in the first of his letters to his friend Lucilius, and there, in Richard Gummere's translation, it's one line: "Nothing, Lucilius, is ours, except time." Your house can be taken, your money can be lost. Time is the one thing that was put in your hands alone. And it's the one thing nobody ever returns. Seneca doesn't say never give your time away. Friendship, service, love: those take hours, and they're worth it. His point is about the ledger. Know where it goes. Choose where it goes. Guard at least one hour the way you'd guard your wallet.
screen: `NOT AN INCH OF LAND.` · `WILDLY GENEROUS WITH TIME.` · `GO THROUGH THE LEDGER.` · `NOTHING IS OURS, EXCEPT TIME.` · then, large: `GUARD ONE HOUR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then picture tomorrow as a ledger, hour by hour. Morning, midday, afternoon, evening. Notice which hours are already spoken for. Then find one hour you could guard. Not for work. For something you'd truly choose: a walk, a friend, a book, rest. Picture yourself protecting it. Saying no, kindly, to what would take it. The bell holds the time.
The ledger of hours. Seneca's reminder that we guard our money and give our time away, when time is all that's truly ours.
Your line: time is the only property. Tomorrow, guard one hour. Put it in your calendar if that helps, and give it only to something you choose. Day thirty-one.

howItsDone: People who follow Seneca's advice often keep an account of their time, as he told Lucilius he did, and deliberately protect some hours for what they value most.
